beats.say: You were born with about three hundred bones.
beats.cap: YOU WERE BORN WITH | ABOUT *300 BONES.*

beats.say: Now you have two hundred and six.
So where did the rest go?
They didn't fall out. They fused.
As a baby grows, small bones join together into bigger ones.
beats.cap: AS A BABY GROWS, | SMALL BONES *JOIN* | INTO BIGGER ONES.

beats.say: And many of them start out as soft cartilage,
beats.cap: AND MANY START OUT | AS SOFT *CARTILAGE,*

beats.say: Even your kneecaps start as cartilage.
They're not fully developed until around age ten to twelve.
beats.cap: NOT FULLY DEVELOPED | UNTIL AROUND | *AGE 10 TO 12.*

beats.say: So you didn't lose any bones.
Your skeleton just did a merger.

sources.fact: Cleveland Clinic, 'How Many Bones Do Babies Have?': a newborn has 275 to 300 bones, while most adults have 206; as a baby grows, their smaller bones join together to create larger bones; many baby bones start as cartilage and fuse and harden through ossification

Cleveland Clinic, '15 Facts About Your Bones and Skeletal System': you were born with around 300 bones and have 206 now; your skeleton fuses together as you grow; kneecaps start as cartilage that hardens over time and are not fully developed until around age 10 or 12

Popular Science, 'You'll never have as many bones as you did at birth': newborns can have more than 300 distinct bones; the extra bones fuse together as they develop, starting as cartilage that bone cells ossify; the adult skeleton has 206 bones

math.note: Cleveland Clinic: born with around 300 bones (275 to 300)
Cleveland Clinic: most adults have 206 bones
Cleveland Clinic: kneecaps fully developed around age 10 or 12 (low end)
Cleveland Clinic: kneecaps fully developed around age 10 or 12 (high end)

post.instagram_caption:
You were born with about 300 bones. Now you have 206 🦴

They didn't fall out. As a baby grows, small bones join together into bigger ones, and many start as soft cartilage that slowly hardens into bone. Even your kneecaps start as cartilage and aren't fully developed until around age 10 to 12.

So you didn't lose any bones. Your skeleton just did a merger.

Sources: Cleveland Clinic, Popular Science.
